questions.question: What are Java keywords and can you use them as variable names?
questions.title: Java Reserved Keywords — What They Are and Why You Can't Use Them
questions.direct_answer: **Java keywords** are reserved words with special meaning in the language syntax — about **67 reserved words** including `int`, `class`, `return`, `static`, `final`, `if`, `for`, `new`, `this`, `super`. They **cannot** be used as variable, method, or class names because the compiler treats them as language constructs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Java language literacy and awareness of syntax rules every Java developer must know from day one
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that true, false, and null are technically literals (not keywords) but are equally reserved, or trying to use keywords like 'class' or 'int' as names
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that var and yield are context-sensitive keywords — they can be names in some contexts but act as keywords in others, unlike strict keywords which are always reserved

sections.title: A Keyword Is a Word Java Has Already Claimed for Itself
sections.content:
**A keyword is a word that Java has reserved for itself**, like `class`, `if`, or `return`. The language gives each of these words one fixed meaning, and that meaning never changes.

Why does Java need them? The compiler reads your source code **one word at a time**. It needs certain words to always mean the same thing so it can tell a command apart from a name you invented. If you could rename `return`, the compiler would have no way to know when a method is actually finishing.

So here is how it plays out. When the compiler sees `int`, it knows a whole-number variable is being declared. When it sees `class`, it knows a class is starting. Because these words are **already taken**, you cannot reuse them as your own variable, method, or class names — that is a compile error. It is like English grammar: you can name a shop 'Oak Bakery', but not 'The' or 'And', because those words already do a job in the sentence.

For an interview, know the rough counts. Java has **52 strict keywords** that are always reserved — `class`, `int`, `if`, `for`, `static`, `final`, and so on. It also has about **15 reserved words** like `const` and `goto` that Java set aside but never actually used; `const` exists, yet you write `final` in its place.

> The gotcha most people miss: `true`, `false`, and `null` look like keywords but are technically **literals** — built-in fixed values. You still cannot name a variable `true`, but calling them keywords in an interview is a small spec slip. Newer words like `var` and `yield` are **context-sensitive** — they act as keywords only in certain spots, so old code that used `var` as a field name still compiles.

sections.title: How Java Classifies Reserved Words
sections.content:
Here is how the ~67 reserved words break into categories. The left branch covers words that always prevent their use as identifiers; the right branch covers the newer context-sensitive words that are more flexible. ```mermaid flowchart TD R["Java Reserved Words (~67 total)"] R --> SK["Strict keywords (52)
always reserved
class, int, if, for, return..."] R --> RU["Reserved but unused (15)
const, goto
reserved, not implemented"] R --> LIT["Literals (3)
true, false, null
not keywords but still off-limits"] R --> CSK["Context-sensitive keywords
var, yield, record, sealed...
keyword in some spots, name in others"] SK --> RULE1["Using them as names
= compile error"] RU --> RULE2["const → use final instead
goto → not available"] LIT --> RULE3["Can't name a variable true
or false or null"] CSK --> RULE4["var triggers type inference
but old code can still have
a field named var"] ``` The key insight from this diagram: strict keywords are the absolute no-go zone. Context-sensitive keywords are the flexible newer additions Java introduced carefully to stay backward compatible.

sections.title: Keywords vs Literals at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Strict keywords|~52 always reserved|class, int, return|static, final, if|never identifiers
blue|Reserved unused|~15 reserved words|const, goto|reserved, not implemented|use final, not const
emerald|Literals|~true, false, null|technically not keywords|still can't be names|fixed values
rose|Context-sensitive|~var, yield|keyword in some spots|identifier elsewhere|added without breaking old code

sections.title: Why These Three Lines Refuse to Compile
sections.content:
Each line below tries to bend a reserved word into a name. Watch what the compiler does with them.

```java
int class = 5;        // COMPILE ERROR: 'class' is a keyword
String return = "x";  // COMPILE ERROR: 'return' is a keyword
boolean true = false; // COMPILE ERROR: 'true' is a literal, still off-limits
```

The errors here are famously cryptic — Java doesn't say "that's a keyword." The moment it reads `class` it tries to start a class definition, so it reports something like *'class, interface, or enum expected'*. Once you learn to recognize that an accidental keyword is the cause, these confusing messages stop being mysterious.

sections.title: The Same Words, Now Used Legally
sections.content:
Flip every illegal line into a working one and a pattern emerges — you can name things *around* keywords, just not *with* them.

```java
int userCount = 5;        // valid identifier
int var = 100;            // 'var' is context-sensitive — valid as a name here
boolean isActive = true;  // 'true' is a literal; 'isActive' is a valid name
final int MAX = 10;       // 'final' is a keyword; 'MAX' is a valid name
```

The `var` line is the surprising one. Because `var` is context-sensitive, it is perfectly legal as a variable name even though `var x = 5;` would trigger type inference. Strict keywords like `final` never get that flexibility — but notice you can still build a name like `MAX` while `final` itself stays reserved.

sections.title: A Runnable Snapshot of the Rules Together
When This Knowledge Matters
sections.content:
- When **naming variables, methods, and classes** — your IDE flags keyword usage, but understanding why prevents frustration.
- During **debugging**, cryptic syntax errors sometimes mean you used a keyword as an identifier.
- In **legacy code** you'll see workarounds like `clazz` because developers needed class-like names.
- In **interviews**, knowing the difference between strict keywords, context-sensitive keywords, and reserved literals signals foundational language knowledge.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling `true`, `false`, and `null` keywords**: they are *literals*, not keywords. The practical effect is identical — you still can't name a variable `true` — but stating it wrong in an interview signals you memorized a list instead of understanding the spec.
- **Reaching for `const` out of C/C++ habit**: `const` is reserved but never implemented, so `const int X = 5;` simply won't compile. Java's constant keyword is `final`.
- **Forgetting words are context-sensitive**: legacy code may have a field literally named `var` or `yield`, and that's legal — but `var x = 5;` in the same file triggers type inference. Knowing which words are strict and which bend to context is exactly what separates a confident answer.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **52 strict keywords** — always reserved (`class`, `int`, `return`, ...).
- **15 reserved words** — reserved but unused (`const`, `goto`).
- **Literals** — `true`, `false`, `null` aren't keywords but are reserved.
- **Context-sensitive** — `var`, `yield` are keywords only in certain spots.
- **Compile-time enforcement** — using a keyword as a name fails to compile.
- **Case-sensitive** — `class` is reserved; `Class` (the type) is not.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Think of keywords as **words Java has already claimed** for its own grammar — the second the compiler sees `class` or `return`, it reads them as instructions, so you simply can't reuse them as variable, method, or class names.

There are **67 reserved words** in all: 52 strict keywords, plus around 15 like `const` and `goto` that Java set aside but never implemented, which is why people from a C background reach for `const` where Java wants `final`.

One distinction worth getting right is that `true`, `false`, and `null` feel like keywords but are actually **literals** — you still can't name a variable `true`, yet knowing they're literals shows you understand the spec rather than a memorized list.

What really sharpens the answer is **context-sensitive keywords** like `var` and `yield`: they behave as keywords only in certain positions, so legacy code with a field named `var` still compiles. Strict keywords are always off-limits; context-sensitive ones bend to where they sit.

questions.question: What does the static keyword mean in Java and where can it be applied?
questions.title: static Keyword in Java — Fields, Methods, Blocks, and Nested Classes
questions.direct_answer: The **`static`** keyword means a member belongs to the **class itself**, not to any individual object. A static field is **shared across all instances**; a static method can be called **without creating an object**. Static members load once when the class loads and persist for the program's lifetime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of class-level versus instance-level members — a foundational distinction in nearly every Java codebase
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to access instance variables from a static method (compile error), or thinking static methods are overridden polymorphically when they're actually hidden
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain static initializer blocks that run once at class load, that static methods are hidden not overridden, and give Math/Collections as real-world utility examples

sections.title: static Means the Member Belongs to the Class, Not to Any Object
sections.content:
The `static` keyword means a field or method **belongs to the class itself**, not to any single object you create from it. There is exactly one copy of it, and that one copy is shared by everything.

Why is that useful? Normally every object keeps its own private copy of each field — three `BankAccount` objects mean three separate balances. But sometimes you want **one value that all objects share**, or a method you can call without building an object first. That is exactly the gap `static` fills.

Here is how it works. A **static field** is a single shared box at the class level; every object reads and writes that same box. A **static method** is called straight on the class name — you write `Math.sqrt(25)`, never `new Math().sqrt(25)`. Picture a company: each employee has their own salary and desk (instance data), but the company name and address are shared by everyone at once (static data).

A couple of details matter in interviews. Static members load into memory once, when the class is first loaded, before any object exists, and they stay until the program ends. A **static initializer block** lets you run one-time setup at that moment, and `static` can also sit on a nested class.

> The gotcha freshers hit: a `static` method runs without any particular object, so it has no `this`. That means it cannot read instance fields directly — the compiler rejects it, because there is no object to ask *whose* value to return. And static methods are **hidden, not overridden**: the reference type decides which version runs, so polymorphism does not apply.

sections.title: Static Variable Shared vs Instance Variable Per-Object
sections.content:
This diagram shows the core idea visually. The static variable `count` lives once at the class level. Each instance has its own `balance`. All three instances share the same `count`. ```mermaid flowchart TD CLS["BankAccount class
────────────────
static int count = 3
(one shared copy)"] OBJ1["account1 object
────────────────
double balance = 500.0
String owner = Alice"] OBJ2["account2 object
────────────────
double balance = 1200.0
String owner = Bob"] OBJ3["account3 object
────────────────
double balance = 800.0
String owner = Carol"] OBJ1 -- reads/writes --> CLS OBJ2 -- reads/writes --> CLS OBJ3 -- reads/writes --> CLS CLS --> NOTE["All three objects see count = 3
Changing count via one object
changes it for all others too"] ``` This is the mental model that unlocks everything about static: one shared box at the class level, versus separate per-object boxes for instance variables.

sections.title: static at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|static field|~One shared copy|belongs to the class|all instances share it|loaded once at class load
blue|static method|~Call without an object|Math.sqrt(25)|no this reference|can't touch instance members
emerald|static block|~One-time setup|runs at class load|before any instance|load tables / libraries
rose|Inheritance|~Hidden, not overridden|reference type decides|no polymorphism|utility classes use static

sections.title: The Error Every Beginner Hits With static
Why This Version Compiles: static Talking to static
All Four Flavors of static in One Class
When to Use Static Members
sections.content:
- Use **static methods** for utility functions with no object state — `Math.max()`, `Collections.sort()`, your own `StringUtils.isEmpty()`.
- Use **static fields** for constants (`static final`) and counters.
- Use **static factory methods** like `Optional.of()` or `LocalDate.now()` for descriptive creation.
- Use **static initializer blocks** for one-time setup at class load (loading native libraries, lookup tables).

Avoid `static` for business logic that needs instance data.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading instance fields from a static method**: static code has no `this`, so `static double getBalance() { return balance; }` won't compile — there's no object to read `balance` from. Make the field static, or accept an instance as a parameter.
- **Expecting static methods to be overridden**: they're *hidden*, not overridden. If a parent and child both declare `static void load()`, the reference type decides which runs — `Parent.load()` calls the parent's version even on a child object. Polymorphism simply doesn't apply.
- **Hoarding state in static fields**: every static field is shared, global, mutable state — hard to unit-test in isolation, and a race condition waiting to happen the moment two threads write to it without synchronization.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Class-level ownership** — one copy shared by all instances.
- **No instance access** — static methods can't touch instance members directly.
- **Called without objects** — `ClassName.method()`.
- **Static blocks** — run once at class load for setup.
- **Hidden, not overridden** — static methods don't use polymorphism.
- **Utility pattern** — `Math`, `Collections`, `Arrays` are static-only.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Picture ten `BankAccount` objects: each keeps its own balance, but they can all share a **single counter or bank name** marked `static` — one copy that lives on the class rather than on any object. You call `static` methods straight on the class, like `Math.sqrt(25)`, with no `new Math()` involved.

The snag people hit is that a `static` method **can't read instance fields** or call instance methods, because it runs with no particular object — there's no `this` for it to reach through, so the compiler stops you.

`static` members **load once** when the class loads and stick around for the whole program, and a `static` initializer block is where you do one-time setup at that point.

The detail that stands out is that `static` methods are **hidden, not overridden** — `Parent.method()` runs the parent's version even on a child object. That's exactly why utility classes like `Math` and `Collections` are pure `static`: their work needs no object state at all.

questions.question: What does the final keyword mean when applied to a class or a method in Java?
questions.title: final Class and final Method in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **`final` class** cannot be extended — no subclasses allowed. A **`final` method** cannot be overridden by subclasses. These restrictions enforce critical behavior — `String`, `Integer`, and all wrapper classes are `final` to guarantee immutability and security across the Java ecosystem.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of final in its three forms — variable, method, class — and the design intent behind preventing inheritance or overriding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing final variable (constant) and forgetting final class and final method exist, or not understanding why you'd prevent inheritance
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that String and wrappers are final for immutability/security, and that final methods enable inlining by avoiding virtual dispatch

sections.title: A final Class Can't Be Extended, a final Method Can't Be Overridden
sections.content:
A `final` class is a class that **no other class is allowed to extend**, and a `final` method is a method that no subclass is allowed to override. Most people first meet `final` on a variable, where it makes a constant — but it does these two more things as well.

Why would you ever block subclassing? Because sometimes **a class is finished**. Its design is complete and correct, and letting someone build on top of it could quietly break a promise it makes. `final` lets you lock that promise in.

Here is how each form behaves. Put `final` on a class and any `extends` of it becomes a **compile error** — the inheritance chain stops there. Put `final` on a method and subclasses still inherit it and can call it, but they cannot replace it with their own version. The behavior is frozen.

This shows up everywhere in real Java. `String` is a `final` class on purpose: nobody can write a mutable subclass that overrides `equals` or `hashCode`, which is what keeps a `String` safe as a `HashMap` key. `Integer` and the other wrapper types are final for the same reason. Final methods fit the **template-method pattern**, where a final method fixes the overall steps while the individual steps it calls stay overridable.

> The gotcha to remember: a final class is **not** the same as an immutable one. `StringBuilder` is a final class, yet every `append` changes its contents. Real immutability needs final fields and no setters — `final` on the class alone only stops inheritance, not change.

sections.title: Decision Flowchart for final Class and final Method
sections.content:
Use this diagram to reason through what final blocks. The left branch answers 'can a subclass extend this class?' and the right branch answers 'can a subclass override this method?' ```mermaid flowchart TD Q1["Is the class marked final?"] Q1 -- Yes --> A1["No subclassing allowed
Compile error if you try to extend
Examples: String, Integer, StringBuilder"] Q1 -- No --> A2["Subclassing allowed
Child classes can extend it"] A2 --> Q2["Is the method marked final?"] Q2 -- Yes --> B1["Cannot be overridden
Subclass inherits it as-is
Example: final void log()"] Q2 -- No --> B2["Can be overridden
Subclass can redefine it
Example: void process()"] B1 --> NOTE1["Guarantees consistent behavior
Used for security-critical methods
and template method skeletons"] A1 --> NOTE2["Guarantees no broken subclass
Protects immutability and
hashCode/equals contracts"] ``` The pattern is simple: final on a class blocks going deeper in the hierarchy; final on a method blocks replacing that specific behavior while still letting the class be extended.

sections.title: final Class and Method at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|final class|~Cannot be extended|no subclasses|String, Integer, wrappers|design is sealed
blue|final method|~Cannot be overridden|inherited but fixed|guarantees behavior|enables inlining
emerald|Why|~Security + correctness|String immutability|protect invariants|template method skeleton
rose|Not immutability|~final class != immutable|StringBuilder is final + mutable|need final fields|and no setters

sections.title: What Happens the Moment You Extend a final Class
sections.content:
Mark a class final and the door to inheritance closes — here's what the compiler does when someone tries to walk through it anyway.

```java
public final class SecurityUtil { /* sealed */ }
class Custom extends SecurityUtil { } // COMPILE ERROR: can't extend a final class
```

The `extends` line fails before the program ever runs. Marking `SecurityUtil` final tells the compiler the inheritance chain stops right here — nobody can slip in a subclass that overrides its methods and quietly weakens whatever security guarantee it was built to protect.

sections.title: Locking One Method While Leaving the Rest Open
The Standard Recipe for a Bulletproof Utility Class
When to Use Final Classes and Methods
sections.content:
Use **final classes** for:

- **utility classes** (only static methods, like `Math`)
- **immutable value classes** (subclassing would break immutability — that's why `String` is final)
- **security-sensitive classes**

Use **final methods** in:

- **template method patterns** (a final method orchestrates overridable steps)
- **correctness-critical methods** (authorization checks, cleanup)
- **performance-critical hot paths**

Avoid overusing `final` — use it intentionally, not defensively.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Knowing only final variables**: `final` also seals classes and methods. If you can only talk about constants, you've answered just a third of the question — interviewers ask `final` precisely to see if you know the other two forms.
- **Not knowing why `String` is final**: if you could subclass `String` and override `equals()`/`hashCode()`, every `HashMap` and `HashSet` keyed on strings could silently return wrong results. The language forbids the subclass to protect that contract.
- **Confusing final class with immutability**: a final class can still mutate. `StringBuilder` is final, yet every `append()` changes its contents. Real immutability needs final fields and no setters — final on the class alone doesn't give it to you.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **final class** — cannot be extended.
- **final method** — cannot be overridden.
- **Design decision** — for completeness, security, or correctness.
- **String/wrappers final** — for immutability and value semantics.
- **Performance** — final methods can be inlined.
- **Not immutability** — final class ≠ immutable instances.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The way I'd frame it is that `final` **locks down a guarantee**. A `final` class can't be extended, so the inheritance chain stops, and a `final` method can't be overridden, so subclasses inherit it exactly as written.

The **textbook case** is `String`: it's `final` precisely so nobody can slip in a mutable subclass that overrides `equals` or `hashCode` and quietly break every `HashMap` and `HashSet` keyed on strings. `Integer` and the other wrappers are `final` for that same value-semantics reason.

In practice you see `final` classes on utility types like `Math`, and `final` methods in the **template-method pattern**, where the `final` method pins the overall algorithm while the steps it calls stay overridable — it can even let the JVM inline the call, since there's no override to dispatch to.

The trap I'd flag is **assuming `final` means immutable**. It doesn't — `StringBuilder` is `final` yet fully mutable. `final` stops inheritance and overriding, usually for security, correctness, or a design that's meant to stay complete.

questions.question: What does public static void main(String[] args) mean in Java?
questions.title: public static void main(String[] args) — Each Keyword Explained
questions.direct_answer: It's the **entry point** of a Java program — the exact method the JVM looks for to start running your code. **`public`** lets the JVM call it from outside the class, **`static`** lets it run without creating an object, **`void`** means it returns nothing, **`main`** is the fixed name the JVM searches for, and **`String[] args`** receives command-line arguments.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate truly understands what each token does rather than having memorized the line by rote
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Knowing the line works but not why each keyword is required — especially why static is needed and what breaks if you drop or rename parts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the exact runtime errors: dropping static gives 'Main method is not static', renaming main gives 'no main method found' / NoSuchMethodError; mention String... args and public static void order flexibility

sections.title: The One Line the JVM Looks For to Start Your Program
sections.content:
`public static void main(String[] args)` is the exact line the JVM looks for to start running a Java program — it is the program's **entry point**. When you run `java MyProgram`, the JVM loads the class and calls precisely this method first. Every beginner copies it on day one; the interview question is whether you know *why* each word is there.

Why does the JVM need such a rigid signature? Because it has to call your code without knowing anything about your class except its name. The signature is **a fixed contract**: if your method matches it exactly, the JVM can find and invoke it; if any piece is off, the JVM has nothing to start from.

Here is what each token does, left to right:

- **`public`** makes the method visible from outside the class so the JVM — which lives outside your code — is allowed to call it.
- **`static`** lets the JVM call `main` without creating an object first; at startup no instance of your class exists yet, so the entry point can't depend on one.
- **`void`** means `main` returns nothing to the JVM — the program signals success or failure through exit codes, not a return value.
- **`main`** is simply the fixed name the JVM searches for; the launcher is hard-coded to look for a method called `main`.
- **`String[] args`** is an array that receives command-line arguments — run `java MyProgram hello 42` and `args` holds `["hello", "42"]`.

The part interviewers probe is **what breaks if you change it**. Drop `static` and the program compiles but fails at launch with *"Main method is not static"*. Misspell `main` or change the parameters and the JVM reports it can't find a `main` method (a `NoSuchMethodError`-style failure) — because it matches the signature literally. You *can* reorder `public` and `static`, rename `args`, or write `String... args` instead, but the four essentials — `public`, `static`, `void`, and the name `main` taking a `String[]` — must all be present.

sections.title: How the JVM Finds and Calls main — Token by Token
sections.content:
Reading the signature the way the JVM does makes each keyword's job obvious. The launcher loads your class, then hunts for one specific method shape before anything in your program runs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    JVM["You run: java MyProgram"] --> LOAD["JVM loads the MyProgram class"]
    LOAD --> FIND["Searches for method named main with String[] parameter"]
    FIND --> P["public · so the JVM can call it from outside the class"]
    FIND --> S["static · so it runs with no object created"]
    FIND --> V["void · returns nothing to the JVM"]
    FIND --> N["main · the exact name the launcher looks for"]
    FIND --> A["String[] args · command-line arguments"]
    P --> RUN["All match -> program starts"]
    S --> RUN
    V --> RUN
    N --> RUN
    A --> RUN
    RUN --> FAIL["Any mismatch -> Main method not static or no main method found"]
```

The takeaway: the JVM matches this method by its literal shape, not by intent. Every token is part of the lock, and the launcher only turns when the whole key fits.

sections.title: The Smallest Complete Java Program
Drop static and It Compiles — Then Refuses to Launch
Add static Back and the JVM Has Its Entry Point
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Dropping `static`**: `public void main(String[] args)` compiles but fails at launch with *"Main method is not static"* — the JVM has no object to call it on at startup. This trips people up because it's a runtime error from code that compiled cleanly.
- **Renaming `main` or changing the parameters**: the launcher searches for the literal name `main` taking a `String[]`. `public static void start(...)` or `main(String args)` (no array) means the JVM can't find a valid entry point — you get a `NoSuchMethodError`-style *"no main method"* failure.
- **Thinking the keyword *order* is fixed**: it isn't. `static public void main(...)` is equally valid — Java allows modifiers in any order. What's fixed is that all of `public`, `static`, `void`, the name `main`, and a `String[]` parameter are present.
- **Assuming `args` can be `null`**: when you run with no arguments, `args` is an *empty* array, not `null`, so `args.length` is `0` — calling `args[0]` without checking throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Entry point** — `main` is the method the JVM calls first when you run the program.
- **`public`** — the JVM lives outside your class, so the method must be visible to be called.
- **`static`** — no object exists at startup, so the JVM calls `main` on the class directly; dropping it gives *"Main method is not static"*.
- **`void`** — `main` returns nothing; success/failure is signalled via exit codes.
- **`main`** — the exact name the launcher searches for; rename it and the JVM can't find an entry point.
- **`String[] args`** — command-line arguments; empty array (not `null`) when none are passed.
- **Order is flexible** — `static public` is fine; the five essentials just all have to be there.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd describe it as **the contract the JVM uses to start your program** — when you run `java MyProgram`, it loads the class and looks for exactly this method. Then I'd walk the tokens. `public` makes it callable from outside the class, and the JVM is outside your code, so it has to be visible. `static` is the **one that really matters**: at startup no object of your class exists yet, so the JVM has to call `main` on the class directly, without creating an instance. `void` means it returns nothing — the program reports success or failure through an exit code, not a return value. `main` is just the fixed name the launcher searches for, and `String[] args` carries the command-line arguments.

Where I'd show I actually understand it is **what breaks**. Drop `static` and it compiles but fails to launch with "Main method is not static." Rename `main` and the JVM can't find an entry point at all. The order of `public` and `static` is flexible, but **those five pieces all have to be there**.
